blocks.text: **The problem.** Given the `root` of a binary tree, return **all root-to-leaf paths**, each written as a string like `"1->2->5"`. A **leaf** is a node with no children.

blocks.alt: The tree 1, 2, 3, null, 5. It has two leaves, 5 and 3, so two root-to-leaf paths: 1->2->5 and 1->3.

blocks.code:
Input:  root = [1, 2, 3, null, 5]
Output: ["1->2->5", "1->3"]

Input:  root = [1]
Output: ["1"]

blocks.text: There is exactly **one path per leaf**, so the job is: walk down, remember the way you came, and write it out each time you reach a leaf. The approaches differ in **how they remember the way**.
1. Brute force: carry a new string down
Pass the path so far as a string. Each node creates a **new** string — the old one plus `->` and its value — and passes it to its children. A leaf adds its string to the answer.
**Time O(n · h), space O(n · h)** in the worst case — every node copies a string as long as its depth, even nodes that aren't leaves.
2. Optimal: remember parents, climb up from each leaf

Copying strings at **every** node is wasteful when only **leaves** produce output. So walk the tree once, recording each node's **parent** and collecting the leaves. Then, for each leaf, climb parent links up to the root, reverse, and join.

blocks.alt: From leaf 5, follow parent links up: 5 to 2 to 1. Reversed, the path reads 1->2->5.

blocks.code:
def binary_tree_paths(root):
    parent = {root: None}
    leaves = []
    stack = [root]
    while stack:                            # one pass: record parents, find leaves
        node = stack.pop()
        if node.left is None and node.right is None:
            leaves.append(node)
        for child in (node.right, node.left):
            if child:
                parent[child] = node
                stack.append(child)
    paths = []
    for leaf in leaves:
        values = []
        n = leaf
        while n is not None:                # climb to the root
            values.append(str(n.val))
            n = parent[n]
        paths.append("->".join(reversed(values)))
    return paths

blocks.text: **Time O(n + L · h)** for L leaves — strings are built only at leaves — but **space O(n)** for the parent map.
3. Best solution: one shared path, backtracking

Keep **one** list of values for the current path. Step onto a node: **push** its value. At a leaf, join the list into a string. Step back off the node: **pop** its value — that's **backtracking**, and it lets every branch reuse the same list.

blocks.alt: The shared path while walking 1, 2, 3, null, 5. At leaf 5 the path is [1, 2, 5] and is recorded. Backtracking pops 5 and 2, then 3 is pushed: [1, 3] is recorded.

blocks.caption: The same path array grows and shrinks; strings are only made at leaves.

blocks.text: **Time O(n + L · h)** — the output itself has L paths of up to h values, so no solution can do better — and **space O(h)** besides the answer. Push on the way down, pop on the way up: this backtracking pattern is the core of every "list all paths" problem.

blocks.alt: Brute force: O(n · h) time, O(n · h) space. Optimal: O(n + L · h) time, O(n) space. Best: O(n + L · h) time, O(h) space.

items: **A node with one child is not a leaf** — `[1, 2]` has one path, `"1->2"`, not two.
**Negative values** — `"-1->-2"`: the minus sign is part of the number.
**Path Sum II** — only the root-to-leaf paths whose values add up to a target (in the Path Sum lesson).
**Sum Root to Leaf Numbers** — read each path as a number and add them up.
**Smallest String Starting From Leaf** — paths read leaf-to-root as letters; return the smallest.
**All Paths From Source to Target** — the same backtracking on a graph.
